Rat Pest Control: Identify & Remove Roof Rats & Norway Rats

By Shaw's Pest Control  ·  Wichita, KS

How to Identify and Control Roof Rats and Norway Rats in Your Kansas Home

If you've heard scratching in your attic at night or found droppings along your basement walls, you're likely dealing with one of two rat species: roof rats or Norway rats. Understanding which type of rat has invaded your home determines the most effective rat pest control strategy. Both species thrive in Kansas, including throughout the Wichita metro area, and they don't wait for an invitation—especially when temperatures drop. At Shaw's Pest Control, we've been helping Kansas homeowners solve rodent problems since 1987, using proven exclusion techniques backed by three State Certifications and Master Tech expertise. This guide walks you through identifying each species, understanding why they target homes during winter months, and knowing when structural exclusion alone isn't enough.

Understanding the Two Rat Species in Kansas: Roof Rats vs Norway Rats

Roof rats and Norway rats behave differently, nest in different areas, and require tailored control approaches. Roof rats (Rattus rattus), also called black rats, are slender, agile climbers with tails longer than their bodies. They typically measure 13–18 inches from nose to tail tip, with sleek black or dark brown fur. These rats prefer elevated spaces—attics, rafters, wall voids near rooflines, and tree branches close to structures.

Norway rats (Rattus norvegicus), sometimes called brown rats or sewer rats, are stockier and more aggressive. They grow 16–20 inches long, with brown or gray fur and tails shorter than their body length. Unlike their climbing cousins, Norway rats are ground dwellers. They burrow along foundations, live in basements and crawl spaces, and nest in dense vegetation near buildings.

Identifying which species you're dealing with matters because roof rats enter through gaps near your roofline—damaged soffit vents, gaps where utility lines penetrate, or unsealed attic vents—while Norway rats exploit foundation cracks, gaps around garage doors, and damaged crawl space vents. The droppings tell the story too: roof rat droppings are banana-shaped and about ½ inch long, while Norway rat droppings are blunt, capsule-shaped, and closer to ¾ inch. Professional pest control services in Wichita can quickly assess entry points and identify species based on behavior patterns and nesting sites.

Why Rats Invade Kansas Homes During Winter Months

Rats don't hibernate. When temperatures drop below freezing, they seek three things: warmth, food, and water—all of which your home provides in abundance. In Kansas, the seasonal shift usually begins in late October and intensifies through January and February. Roof rats follow tree branches that overhang roofs or climb vinyl siding and downspouts to reach attic entry points. Norway rats tunnel along foundations and squeeze through openings as small as ½ inch—about the diameter of a quarter.

Once inside, rats reproduce rapidly. A single female can produce 5–7 litters per year, with 6–12 pups per litter. That means a small rat problem in November can become a severe infestation by February. Rats also cause serious property damage: they gnaw through electrical wiring (creating fire hazards), shred insulation for nesting material, contaminate stored items with urine and feces, and chew through PEX plumbing and ductwork.

Food sources matter too. Rats are attracted to pet food left in garages, birdseed stored in sheds, garbage bins without secure lids, and even fruit that drops from trees in late fall. If you're noticing increased activity, it's not coincidence—it's survival behavior driven by cold weather and diminishing outdoor food sources. Comprehensive pest control strategies address both current infestations and the environmental factors that attract rodents in the first place.

Structural Exclusion: The Most Effective Long-Term Rat Control Method

Trapping and baiting kill existing rats, but exclusion prevents future invasions. Structural exclusion means sealing every potential entry point with materials rats cannot chew through—galvanized steel mesh, copper mesh, concrete, or heavy-gauge hardware cloth. This isn't a caulk-and-hope-for-the-best situation. Rats have incredibly strong jaws and can gnaw through wood, plastic, rubber, aluminum, and even low-quality concrete.

Start with a thorough exterior inspection. Walk your roofline and look for gaps where soffit meets fascia, damaged roof vents, and spaces around plumbing stacks. Check every window well, dryer vent, and foundation crack. For Norway rats, inspect your garage door seal—if you can see daylight underneath, rats can enter. Tree branches should be trimmed back at least 6 feet from your roofline to eliminate roof rat highways.

Interior exclusion is equally important. Seal gaps around pipes under sinks, repair damaged weather stripping on doors leading to garages or basements, and install door sweeps where needed. Attic vents should have ¼-inch hardware cloth behind them, not flimsy plastic screening. Crawl space vents need the same treatment.

Professional exclusion work is an investment, but it's the only permanent solution. DIY attempts often fail because homeowners miss hidden entry points or use materials rats can defeat. If you're in the El Dorado area and suspect structural vulnerabilities, professional pest control in El Dorado includes detailed inspections that identify weaknesses most homeowners overlook.

When to Call a Professional for Rat Pest Control in Wichita

Some homeowners successfully trap one or two rats using snap traps, but if you're hearing activity in multiple areas, finding fresh droppings daily, or noticing a strong musky odor, you're dealing with an established colony. At that point, DIY efforts rarely succeed. Rats are neophobic—they avoid new objects in their environment, including traps. They also learn from each other's mistakes. If one rat dies in a trap, others in the colony may avoid that trap type entirely.

Professional rat pest control starts with a thorough inspection to determine species, population size, entry points, and nesting locations. Technicians with certifications like Shaw's Pest Control's Master Tech designation understand rat behavior well enough to anticipate travel routes and place traps strategically. We use a combination of mechanical traps, monitoring stations, and exclusion work—not just poison bait, which can lead to rats dying inside wall voids and creating odor problems.

Wichita homeowners face unique challenges due to the area's mix of older homes with crawl spaces and newer construction with complex rooflines. According to recent estimates, Wichita's housing stock includes thousands of homes built before 1980, many with foundation cracks and aging building materials that rats exploit. Professional services bring the tools, materials, and expertise to solve the problem correctly the first time, backed by warranties that DIY methods can't match.

Frequently Asked Questions

What attracts rats to my house?

Rats are attracted to food sources (pet food, garbage, birdseed), water (leaky pipes, pet bowls, standing water), and shelter (cluttered garages, overgrown vegetation, woodpiles against foundations). Homes with easy entry points near these resources become prime targets. Eliminating attractants and sealing entry points are equally important for effective rat pest control.

How do I know if I have roof rats or Norway rats?

Roof rats are slender with tails longer than their bodies, nest in attics and upper areas, and leave banana-shaped droppings. Norway rats are stockier with shorter tails, burrow near foundations, nest in basements or crawl spaces, and leave blunt, capsule-shaped droppings. Activity location—high versus low—is the most reliable indicator of species.

Can I use poison to get rid of rats myself?

DIY poison use is risky because rats often die inside walls, attics, or crawl spaces, creating terrible odors and attracting secondary pests like flies. Poison also poses dangers to pets, children, and non-target wildlife. Professional rat pest control uses integrated approaches that minimize these risks while maximizing effectiveness through strategic trap placement and exclusion work.

How much does professional rat control cost?

Professional rat pest control costs vary based on infestation severity, home size, and necessary exclusion work. Initial inspections typically range from free to $150, with treatment plans starting around $200–$400 for minor issues. Severe infestations requiring extensive exclusion and multiple follow-ups can cost $1,000–$2,500. Most companies offer warranties, making professional service more cost-effective than repeated DIY failures.

How long does it take to get rid of rats?

Minor infestations with only a few rats can be resolved in 1–2 weeks with aggressive trapping. Established colonies typically require 3–6 weeks of monitoring, trapping, and exclusion work. Complete elimination depends on sealing all entry points—otherwise, new rats will replace trapped ones. Professional services include follow-up visits to ensure the problem is fully resolved.

Do rats come back after treatment?

Rats return if entry points remain unsealed or if attractants like food sources and water persist. Effective rat pest control combines elimination of current populations with structural exclusion to prevent reentry. Ongoing monitoring and maintenance—like trimming vegetation and inspecting for new foundation cracks—help ensure rats don't return after treatment ends.
